The Latin closes with praeteritique saeculi honorem et miracula reparare rather than the Greek's future enduring reputation.

The Latin sicut his panis aut ceteris barbaris is retained beside the Greek comparison with other barbarians.
The Latin non ignorabant formulation is preserved, including the ensuing forceful resistance and death.
The Latin list here does not independently include slaves; their distinct ensuing account survives in section 131.
Carnium dilacrerationes quas in ludis agebat differs from the Greek κρεανομιῶν, and is retained.
The Latin compresses the Greek explanation of speculative rumours and their different reception, retaining the ensuing fear and judicial reasoning.

The Latin veluti legentem construction is retained beside the Greek mourning demeanour.
The Latin describes pretending to have lost all adornment at the death, while the Greek describes adopting the appropriate mourning display.
The Latin statuas arrutius et loca singula circumibat differs from the Greek personal designation Stelas Arruntius.
The Latin post amissionem anime eius fauorabiles essent differs from the Greek readiness to surrender their own lives for Gaius.
The Latin preserves fear of senatorial power but does not independently repeat the Greek alternative of a newly appointed ruler.

Cuius mali tunc causa fuit altion medicus is retained without correcting the transmitted account.

The Latin condition concerns cooperatores in nece gai, while the Greek condition concerns cooperation in gaining rule.

The Latin closing eo quod non principum cuncta subiciantur remains unchanged.
The Latin preserves the principal comparison and unjust cruelty, with no independent final mention of gods.

The Latin focuses on prohibition of adverse speech and contrary opinion.
Amittentes delectationem pacis is retained beside the Greek submission to the pleasure of peace.
The Latin preserves remembrance, first plan and first risk, without distinct expression of the Greek honour-vote under freedom.
Et celeratura quidem est agnita differs from the Greek destruction of the carving and remains literal.

The Latin lacks an independent hundred-year expression. The final qui senatui consentiebant clause attaches grammatically to prior consuls, although its Greek thematic counterpart belongs to 188; the proposed 188 cut awaits human decision.

The surviving mutual deliberation begins after sufficienter, which completes the previous gratitude clause. The existing paragraph-start label cannot be reused as this exact start.
The Latin speaks of a civil war almost already blazing under Pompey and its quelling, beside the Greek analogy to Pompey's conflict.
Quia sineque mortem temperaret uellet remains literal beside the Greek refusal to learn restraint from Gaius's death.
The Latin retains funeral observance and mourning without independently repeating the Greek report of surviving Gaius and doctors. The existing manuscript III remains an independent source marker.
The Latin quasi abscortu remearet is retained beside the Greek pretext of leaving a convivial gathering.
Conponendam esse huiusmodi causam is the transmitted Latin object of persuasion, rather than a separate explicit surrender of imperial office.
The Latin minucianus ante ponebat differs from the Greek restraint of Valerius Asiaticus's ambitions. The gladiator noun introduces the continuing construction of 253.
The Latin continuing construction begins at turba non parua after the prior gladiator introduction and does not independently name rowers.

The Latin hanc magnanimitatem assequi conpulit differs from the Greek reproach of Chaerea's attachment to life.
